title: The Fed’s Next Chair Faces AI Uncertainty, Political Heat and Credit Risks
content: The Federal Reserve has just cut rates by 25 basis points into an economy it still expects to grow faster next year, raising questions about why it eased and how much further it can go. Former Council of Economic Advisers chair Glenn Hubbard discusses the decision, the neutral rate and why he doesn’t see much more room for rate cuts going into 2026. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Affordability a 2026 Concern: Amalgamated CEO
content: Priscilla Sims Brown, Amalgamated Bank CEO, says most people agree affordability is a major concern. She tells Romaine Bostick and Katie Greifeld on “The Close” that the bank is deeply engaged in its Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy program and that 40% of its lending is climate related. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Airline Azul Wins US Court Approval of Restructuring Plan
content: Brazilian airline Azul SA won US court permission to exit bankruptcy and implement a creditor-backed restructuring that trims debt and lines up new investment from United Airlines Holdings Inc. and American Airlines Group Inc.

title: Overall Spreads Remain Tight Even As Oracle Debt Risk Jumps
content: On "Bloomberg Real Yield", Maureen O'Connor, global head of high-grade debt syndicate at Wells Fargo Corporate & Investment Bank, and Amanda Lynam, head of macro credit research at BlackRock, talks with Matt Miller about credit spreads, issuance and risks tied to the boom in AI growth. There’s a frenzy of development going on to support the AI revolution, and with it an insatiable demand for debt to fund it. Some estimate the overall infrastructure roll-out cost could reach $10 trillion, and with so many lenders lining up to throw cash at the assets, the fear is a bubble is building. (Source: Bloomberg)

title: Clearlake-Backed Newfold Puts Side Deals at the Forefront in Debt Overhaul

title: Wall Street Week | Hubbard on Fed Cut Fallout, Open Source AI, Nuclear Bet, Department Store Revival
content: This week, Glenn Hubbard warns that tariffs, shaky data and a mature credit cycle create risks as the Fed looks toward 2026. And, will open AI ecosystems win out over closed models, as AMD CEO Lisa Su and former IBM CEO Sam Palmisano suggest? Plus, from AI to manufacturing, soaring electricity demand is forcing a rethink of where our power comes from and how fast we can build to generate it. Later, can Macy’s reinvent the department store for today’s shopper? (Source: Bloomberg)

Wie der Angriff auf den Platzhirsch Revolut gelingen und die Kurve beim Aktienkurs (seit dem IPO rund 17 Prozent im Minus) gekratzt werden soll, erklärte Marketingchef David Sandström (42) im Gespräch mit meiner Kollegin Charlotte Rick (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed76e57a31d18d7569e556e7fcb4e694b860a10d9c9a2966093a2ad9bef79419bc8c43fde5ac943b5abe6529d13f0d0184d626c55ceb45aa37c>.

Die Wirtschaftsnews des Tages:

  *   Die Wirtschaftsweisen haben ihre Prognose für das kommende Jahr gesenkt, sie rechnen jetzt mit einem leicht schwächeren Aufschwung als noch im Frühjahr<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed70333e1c7696fdcafbcd733b938ad2b15cd5ba10e869a09d469b9261c07ba1b0dbdb31915196594e1aa81713f28fdb312013ede45e5b7306a>. Zudem richten die Ökonomen einen Appell an die Bundesregierung: Der instabile Bundeshaushalt gefährde eine sinnvolle Verwendung des Sondervermögens.

  *   Bayer ächzt weiter unter der Klagewelle gegen den 2018 übernommenen Saatgutriesen Monsanto. Dennoch gelang es, das operative Ergebnis im Sommerquartal im Jahresvergleich deutlich zu steigern<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed750dc641325a03b3a87593b72c8fba2199a9b7ba9ccece73905f80f2db122ca6ade511fa832894bb863b2e1e42408c0a5491a0e4b1fd01330>. Dazu trugen vor allem niedrigere Herstellungskosten und Einsparungen im Agrargeschäft bei.

  *   PR-Coup für die Autoland AG: Ex-Finanzminister Christian Lindner (46) heuert ab Januar als stellvertretender Vorstandschef bei dem Gebrauchtwagendiscounter an<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed7b166b873e71c75a9e6661110288429fd3147235e69671e610de0951340ac696e4fbff3835f8aa8b7797abce8e6491a14b2363470d04c4b2d>. Für Autolandgründer Wilfried Wilhelm Anclam (68) ist die Personalie mehr als ein PR-Coup. Wir zeigen, wie der neue Chef von Christian Lindner tickt und was er mit dem Auto-Aldi vorhat.<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed7e531598974a63456c66b27f1482fcf13104715206be508d4772fb98e6388dc780fa34898e2b69da6071b588a2c7c373898319423f91a023e>

  *   Die Deutsche Bahn übertrifft sich mal wieder selbst  zur geplanten Sperrung des Kölner Hauptbahnhofs kommt wegen eines Softwarefehlers noch eine zweite Sperrung hinzu<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed75a2b604eaea8dbde893be08ee7352bdd09aac8cee9685192dbc6335f624f3007428e51bb8d2010ceed49eefb3a09002d2a07c430aeaad13b>. Wie lange das Ganze dauern wird, ist einem Bahn-Sprecher zufolge noch unklar. Anders als die Zahl der Betroffenen: Es sind Hunderttausende Reisende.

[separator]
Was Ihnen in Ihrem Unternehmen helfen könnte:

  *   Viele Firmen stecken eine Menge Geld in Technologien, die ihre Angebote einfacher, schneller und smarter an Nutzerbedürfnisse anpassen sollen. Doch bei der Personalisierung gibt es immer noch viel Luft nach oben. Welche neue Kennzahl zeigt, was Vorreiter wie die Musik-App Spotify mithilfe von KI richtig machen, erfahren Sie beim Harvard Business manager (HBm+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed71e2273ee47b3e30796c5faaa1689c30381fbc6e5023569af493893e0686104566278447429bb49ef14fdbc3de2052f488f93f3034022fee9>.

[separator]

  *   David Reger (37) wollte immer etwas mit Autos machen  fand aber keine Lehrstelle als Kfz-Mechatroniker. Stattdessen gründete er 2019 Neura Robotics. Inzwischen ist das Start-up eine der großen Robotikhoffnungen Europas; mit mehr als 1000 Mitarbeiterinnen und Mitarbeitern aus 45 Nationen bereitet Visionär Reger den Einzug seiner humanoiden Roboter in die deutschen Haushalte vor. Kollege Steffen Ermisch hat den Entrepreneur in seiner Metzinger Firmenzentrale besucht (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=c1e3ddef03459ed712447afa464966cde179c5fb2bc1690d50632fd9098937d9e93a47f11eef00c6fd2f098aad039e5ecebaa9a122a09474dddabdea68e54c64>.

Doch als der Kunstmarkt bis Ende 2024 auf das Niveau des Jahres 2010 einbrach, erwischte es auch den am höchsten gehandelten Künstler der Republik. Shareholder voting

It is approximately true that corporations are owned by their shareholders. [1] The managers of the company work for the shareholders, and the shareholders have the ultimate power to hire and fire them and to approve major strategic decisions. In practice, modern public corporations are owned mostly by diversified shareholders who are rationally apathetic<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/KBF7jGLyDol3L3W8eVSvHiE76P5e-jt0hirXK-RMRHWcrjheeEV3_GtWFtZAVxKvKZXGSM16_gMNHrvkqgLTDUZ-ZYsXHp1tmmK91MNku8eB0f3j2_rptOYawFa62DF6BOxPQqlRl98mqF1bkQ9L_MR9FdGmcHOcapJuDCypF1y-PGEzKQDlGc44rg4ygP8g_LmlDhiigLb0ip4BviWaED6HGS6e5LAQbEv5KWDMEG8qPlanWRaMdA2ueuFiT_xiLnS21k6FTGXvzecP4Eo2iYkwyUg3rkHiGmdmcUPetnVjAeW4-3l1m_QHDVEYOK-VStwkvS6vcFfBYlmv8kcwlcG6WUkZI4q6epwgNEzUTU58nVyTM-gGmfK3AA/GCebbGLUuXrGv75BBXGvRiw8L4TjDW-p/14>. If you have $1 million of retirement savings in the S&P 500 index, it would be absolutely insane<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/-uFa2N5etWvBVXF_zO2rc5wCeXG6pmfIMETwUZIuj9Yn9HOTttagOgLD2Wai4QrRq_5yLIhpe0Mbzd_ygGCm-l60aWog8M3nsrV0_OxrW9Z0CkwG0L0xrQind9qXnaTRQT_JlweVc8Uv07gcpjWeLSInUkb2rAh2VZx2L6ExCYo1N3R7g4AJiVOwpA9RbIrvrZ96ZyuikeXwD3rjNT3V4EPwXYJeSd6Es2rOjLZPRqagFxtCKGoHQnHgi0o2hZBB7kmJ3uVtTos5oox81_vge5iLnN4JeHwuy_oze2zbXF1ywRm9GnjzA0A7kVpZ4LKq3jdFnBgW3BwrJfWv4Slwtf8jg_mZtwlbDClOvS1y-0DxTVpgufFoxHFmSg/m2PPS1pKA3CPkdv4x4gnB6tbXRudKDkA/14> for you to spend even five minutes thinking about who should be the chief executive officer of Sealed Air Corp., or how much he should be paid, or what Sealed Airs strategy should be, or what Sealed Air does. Sealed Air represents about 0.016% of your portfolio, so its effect on your well-being is pretty small, and there are 499 other stocks in that portfolio, so you cant pay attention to all of them. And you own about 0.000003% of Sealed Airs stock, so your opinion about anything cannot possibly matter to Sealed Air. [2] Your best bet, with respect to oversight of Sealed Airs management and strategy, is to ignore it completely.

On the other hand Sealed Airs managers cant just run around enriching themselves and ignoring shareholders. There has to be some oversight. It just has to be delegated: The shareholders have to get someone else to oversee the company for them, so they dont have to think about it. And this delegation also has to be pretty thoughtless and automatic: It would be insane for you to spend five minutes thinking about who you should hire to oversee Sealed Air for you.

There are roughly three mechanisms for this, three sets of people to whom shareholders delegate their power over public companies:

  1.  Boards of directors. This is the oldest and most important answer. The board of the company is responsible for the management and oversight of the company. It hires and fires the CEO and makes the strategic decisions, sometimes asking shareholders to vote to ratify them. The board is nominally elected by the shareholders, but in almost every case directors run unopposed: In practice, the board chooses itself, with the current directors deciding whom to add to the board. [3]  Why should you trust the board to oversee the company for you? Well, they do have fiduciary duties to look out for you, and if they do a bad job you can sue them. [4]  They tend to get paid for their board service in company stock, so they are shareholders themselves and will want to look out for shareholders interests. Also, just, one has to assume a certain level of general professionalism in corporate life. These people devote at least several hours a quarter to serving on the board [5] ; they go to meetings and talk to managers; they have impressive resumes and professional reputations and want to be seen doing a good job. The directors understand that their job is to supervise the company on behalf of the shareholders, and mostly they try hard to do that well.
  2.  Professional investment managers. Above, I suggested that if you invest your retirement portfolio in the S&P 500, you are a shareholder of Sealed Air (an S&P 500 company), but probably you arent, at least not directly. Probably if you have $1 million in the S&P 500, its in an index-tracking mutual fund or exchange-traded fund managed by BlackRock Inc. or Vanguard Group or State Street Corp. or another professional asset manager. You delegate the whole problem of picking stocks, buying stocks and supervising the companies to the managers of your fund. If BlackRock wants to buy Sealed Air stock for you, it will. [6] If BlackRock wants to vote to approve Sealed Airs executive compensation on your behalf, it will. You dont care, and shouldnt. BlackRock is run by professionals who do this for a living, and you pay them to do it so you dont have to. And they too want to do a good job, both for general professionalism reasons and also to keep you as a paying customer. And part of their job is meeting with the managers of the companies and making sure that those managers are doing a good job.
  3.  Proxy advisory services. BlackRock is gigantic, and it has enough people and money to spend at least five minutes a year thinking about whether to approve Sealed Airs executive compensation. (Often at big managers these people will work in a separate governance department responsible for thinking about these things, while the portfolio managers who actually pick the stocks will not worry about voting.) But lots of professional investment managers have only billions of dollars under management, not trillions, and it is not necessarily rational for them to put that kind of time into thinking about the Sealed Air compensation vote. Sealed Air might be 0.1% of their portfolio, and they might own 0.003% of its stock instead of 0.000003%, but thats still not enough for their vote to make a difference to Sealed Air or to their returns. They cant, for regulatory and fiduciary-duty and shame reasons, simply throw the Sealed Air proxy statement in the garbage. But they cant, for good sensible time management reasons, read it either. So they outsource this thinking to a proxy advisory service  the big ones are Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis  that does this professionally. ISS and Glass Lewis will skim the Sealed Air proxy and be like sure vote for the comp package and many investment managers will just do what they say.

None of these mechanisms is perfect, and the central point I want to make here is that they dont have to be because the shareholders dont have that much reason to care. People do complain, though. The imperfections are obvious:

  *   The board might get a bit lazy. The directors will tend to be buddies with management, they are often former public-company CEOs themselves, and they might identify more with the managers than with the shareholders. If the CEO is doing a mediocre job, they might be inclined to say ehh good enough lets double her salary, while a zealous shareholder representative might fire her.
  *   The professional investment managers and proxy advisory services might have their own professional biases. For one thing they probably live in New York or Boston and might have different cultural values from other shareholders. And if they have made corporate governance their lifes work, they probably care more about the formalities and norms of corporate governance than the average shareholder would. It is empirically the case<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/6pwPQn4T2fuQccWJAZcmPThbtkbIF-2gMtaa3Cs42Juk7i6OyVGvJxu4EjTbVL9MIx5m6PrQY_FWhJso_abS6e9TzR6iKBcc7HRWT8JbgV5YcZdPuygITLypGsKHA1xVLquMQrt5OLfJ3V28tI8zOU8_LP9_ic1EMT2_IuSWD8EjSgzOJNmyBzJcYlQpcAGJwAbOUt2G-V8sKgEJJ2vQtDe7PCHAEvgcCfrcWkjsXRXBfbj-Bygy3oDp1GB83kA0y02Ei0EaL1r5xP-cLUFsf2dtuGMytagHmKaWDu-0Cvu4H7K34XUO5EqD_QJEP1We85crQE5kcuZDYwmtEK3YBum-baodKoT9fpNegbGNgfZdem6H2SiVbKBHivk/jLcyzS-V-gfR9Ca4V-8h0gcSRbkd4xGt/14> that (1) a majority of Tesla Inc. shareholders would like to pay Elon Musk $1 trillion to build robots but (2) ISS and Glass Lewis disagree. Paying a CEO $1 trillion sounds cool to the average Tesla shareholder, but sounds distasteful to someone who has made a career of trying to exercise oversight over CEOs. Also, the shareholder advisers, unlike corporate managers and directors, generally dont have skin in the game: They dont get richer if the stock goes up, so they might vote for policies that they personally like even if theyre bad for the bottom line. [7]

This stuff has become a culture-war issue, in part because it genuinely intersects with culture-war controversies  sometimes shareholders will be asked to vote on environmental or social proposals, and proxy advisers will have to take a politically charged position  and in part because CEOs tend to dislike interference from shareholders and so use culture-war rhetoric as a way to limit shareholder power. It is broadly though not always accurately assumed that professional investment managers and proxy advisers are relatively woke and left-wing, and so limiting their power  and putting more power in the hands of the board  is the right-wing move.

And so in Donald Trumps presidency there have been efforts to shift power to boards of directors. We talked about the Securities and Exchange Commissions guidance cracking down on shareholder proposals<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/USDPvL1cEN39curNn_Nqt28UR4I3XZJWNEiW5GmF97c4TBgqn05CGb-kgx1xXIG8V5VCE-asXU2nOyq47D3LzeiHNbXeywkAv1wd1P8kT2qlMPLf8LeUiNp5zkpAYePZz0c5i0Oc40tW6_9v_fxYl70O5-yX0k270WRt5IvOMkDM3LSsg7EQwAgWWoVaTt5UohIIvWYSvH9hm21yXZmidnK7nIBzo2mbNxs8tES6gZnk4A_mXyBjvAJORPkJ8bvCda9jHbeAFAMI90WXa4Z-9CVu9dXmt1tnlmxZS9c2sNvbWT5JeGKdwXoj7VhKloROkuPQOB33CLQNKpgwAKkVukBBTluqdPLjAIM3Rdj2MMRltD_uj9zfCsilgoo/2ofEjuWSH9acvccnG8q4mRPDQrYQpndN/14>, because those proposals tend to give more power to investment managers and proxy advisers.

And in September, Exxon Mobil Corp., with the SECs approval, achieved the dream of every public company: It launched a program in which retail shareholders can delegate their votes to the board<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/BgrUaQMrqDYkHBT9jvOzBFQaR3HhmHcRUX86CyX9fc8CY0LqaNWWQQSRTYXLczv6DrN9C6c0N6Ilvy7NGdyakG-x1ubP5ZsHKe6J2l3K21gMB_h6LNaDk1O_2HT3wf1CZJqamGOcX0USripWa-pDQSMIgJU_4Hv7yC8vM9b-0LXQ_4O90zcLEw7rhCp7sAxEr_2vim_lN4E9DCJYXME6nkGgwbhRcB-2acW3uUyOnF8GSTpFiQaISMPJs1vP6ABKEkUWSXpI2jtGHQ4X3fhSGQDjuQuHkB2-Xm-sXYz28v94pLZ32e94YUZWS4IZVKUsCsj11gI8xi8piUf3WfZe_jqipXNRq3NurjaArQhSXDUC25YrLKo9x_-QpFo/e_QB3oIMBFApDCHPv_LOTWFDoCHvoVrl/14>. Exxon said<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/atIsIcUpJiY8T1h0_sL16XQ3n4ZW2q_gjltWW4vahyOIB0SQa7ZkrFWj-tjaCWiM69LvR-6VEZXcORLgmFObXPpYjsgYFQvjsmbUSstEbGklRrNEtMyiGj948Wgt8mxq80SLtbxvBydNIrkMMDrCYc9pmBCsgj3MRzQJCHusz0N_zaiQmWsfgoVRnTOJO7C45wtkDkfqCwDoOuONv_2WtoeCyhzlUuacW-qSdBdRf2LqIF9mRTa08o5wiBIo7C-329JjjsOsBOaa7uksDbIz13yXt0Qf0CkJidM8zG8L44H9WpAoHwntuLeI2CfIigTwG8-EyPNMM-1uyrfVNRfLmrLS4RlQVhvMhXdJHYL-MPw0zP64nMpY5-vqygg/Us12lsGeELAb39GKW2KyBoGPM_YoNkK2/14>:

ExxonMobils retail investors, many of whom are retired and depend on ExxonMobils dividends to support their livelihoods, have voiced significant frustration over the annual time commitment required to vote at our meetings of shareholders. Each year, retail investors face a large number of proposals to vote on. This burden is not just a matter of hours spent; it also disproportionately impacts retail investors who lack access to professionals dedicated to voting. This limits their participation in shareholder democracy.

Yes, it is insane to participate in shareholder democracy, and now they dont have to. Of course they didnt have to before: In practice, retail shareholders mostly didnt vote, which meant that the votes of professional investment managers and proxy advisers carried more weight. Now the retail shareholders can automatically vote with the board, somewhat diluting those professional votes.

But for most companies the real prize is not to get retail shareholders to go along with whatever the board wants, but to get index funds to go along with whatever the board wants. Today the Wall Street Journal reports<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/95YzZzvjvz5yCELqsP-R0918tASLpelr4yHxYeEsBtIiAnzfr8bUjtODJ79VkKH294m20tbmkEBUA0K1qm5aKHj9BV4QCeDqAT4WQercgsVXk1utrGJ5i8lHyh1C1WWoHNmPhLSpNib51jzjfI-3AMKc6wYayWIfzu-TzCYPzPnWKPO3yPw3FXr8m2fCV3K-d--vXvSXHjihHVZ9TiQ52sIrjYPDzoIcThgqLIB1fT4c4WHD19f7LspMQgn1hKoXrShXMOsr7OkQrm-qhS_BExmsc6uOpQIAKwKKll3daL8a1zQ7OHXMreYA0iblZBAbwpmOzcLkg1mzOMbf63R2mUElPUOdyhvCVl2xrVTQOvsfA3Vz3tWznplMnzQ/WDrdbML93-IsrKV91jswUSBQNr-Xj1tT/14>:

The White House is exploring new measures to curb the influence of proxy advisers and index-fund managers, wading into a hot-button debate raised by high-profile CEOs including Elon Musk and Jamie Dimon in recent months.

Trump administration officials are discussing at least one executive order that would restrict proxy-advisory firms such as Institutional Shareholder Services and Glass Lewis, people familiar with the matter said. That could include a broad ban on shareholder recommendations or an order blocking recommendations on companies that have engaged proxy advisers for consulting work, the people said.

Officials also are exploring limits on how index-fund managers are allowed to vote, seeking to curtail the power of such behemoths as BlackRock, Vanguard Group and State Street, the people said. These three together own on behalf of clients roughly 30% or more of many of the biggest U.S. publicly traded companies. One measure being discussed would require these index-fund managers to mirror their votes in line with clients who choose to vote. 

ISS and Glass Lewis provide recommendations to asset managers on how to vote on shareholder ballots on topics ranging from executive pay packages to environmental goals. Musk recently lashed out at the firms when they recommended a no vote on his historic $1 trillion pay package. Tesla shareholders approved the plan last week.

From first principles it really is obvious that direct and indirect shareholders of public companies should outsource most of their voting decisions to specialized professionals: Individual shareholder votes basically dont matter. But if they do all outsource their voting to the same professionals, then those aggregated votes do matter, at least sometimes, at least symbolically. (Musk got his money!) And so there will be fights over who gets to make the voting decisions, and what decisions they should make.

Total portfolio approach

One of the great intellectual discoveries of modern finance is that, for many purposes, you can treat every stock as a combination of statistical factors. The traditional way to think about a stock is to analyze the companys financial statements, sample its products, talk to its customers, meet with the chief executive officer to evaluate her handshake firmness, and form a view on its prospects and valuation. And then if the stock goes up, you will explain that with reasons like sales of the new product were strong or the CEO was able to cut marketing costs without affecting sales or some other company-specific narrative reason.

And then there is the modern factor approach where you analyze a stock by saying, like, it tends to go up when value stocks go up, and when small-cap stocks go up, and its coefficient on the value factor is X, and its coefficient on the size factor is Y, and its coefficient on the CEO handshakefulness factor is Z, and so on down the line, decomposing each stock into its historical correlation to various statistical factors and themes. I mean, you dont analyze the stock like that; your computer does. Your computer regresses all the stocks against some sensible list of factors. And then if the stock goes up, you will explain that with reasons like the value factor outperformed today or whatever, some statistical market-wide set of stories.

There are all sorts of uses and implications of this in the stock market. Quant hedge funds are doing some form of this, analyzing thousands of stocks to figure out their common drivers and then betting that some drivers will do well. Smart beta funds do versions of this cheaply and at scale, and big multistrategy hedge funds track their factor exposures to make sure that their portfolio managers are not just picking factors: To earn your keep as a modern fundamental equity portfolio manager, you cant just make a big bet on the value factor; you have to add some idiosyncratic insight.

Or we talked once<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/AJsgj84GC6NuEL9voLQqZ5lG486As9yI6TCp91aAFwh7hbOxcVjsSyGT0V30anvQMVefwCERjpF8WQ_Z-xuHyIQ6uU2xcJapkezgitVe_PTAsuScxMFBZU3Un4BNd_BkZ4awXanVniJvP2PRZbHrlp1QWe9pPqnoKjn6FcJzm_tLJz-DJabET5zNgfpijqIf6zsaR8frdB-wpPIYcmmh7IYOGOnNFMpSKVufdnYoM41TmC6QYffo1--vTTGxEOxkAed1val4x3bR2rPCcq0qmO0V8dqnh4OVa0CfV-ZIpQ5CnYfn0Zx2dSj8GkCmmsGYuScn2cxlau3EfIjr-DXqpNwrYEBJ2OB9hxDd0WsRtfhw9XSN7VEUVvuN4v0/fXJgo8xNl4bvtW1GmGW-3_Y_6lJk8eAR/14> about the tax-aware long-short strategy, which basically involves buying $130 of some stocks and short-selling $30 of stocks that are (1) different stocks but (2) statistically the same, so that you get market performance on $100 worth of stock but generate some tax losses. That product makes no sense if you think well I want to buy all the good stocks and short the bad stocks; that product only makes sense if you think ehhh all the stocks are kind of made up of the same basic statistical exposures.

The worry was that banks were less willing to buy and sell bonds for their own balance sheets, so if you had to sell a bond, who would buy it? It turns out, I wrote, that the big proprietary trading firms will increasingly intermediate bond trades, and also, more surprisingly, bond exchange-traded funds can help with the job. That is also in part a story about factor analysis: The quantitative prop trading firms are willing to buy some bonds from sellers, and sell different bonds to buyers, because they have reasonable statistical confidence that the bonds they are selling are essentially the same as the ones they are buying. Here are Bloombergs Justina Lee and Lu Wang on the total portfolio approach<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/uHbYRY5hLLmqJAYXRTqeVyZBI4PLEQSEVQfCfCXFwVwJtseYfdOqLejk5qAtgKaTeGNEyQlmPb5dMwodkou06Q3IAtUYQMid5KZi95HVfxs9ZtIrIJMz6uJTRA_aHZRwGaxxIYjAxYhZvqFzyYLIMGQx5Ps6FtNWWnNWq9akLrutbbOB6B08NUfYw0kN1aetYPTA78FDgc7z_EUvRGtUChaADJugf6DJQbueGz0Yto8-mnd-aXIPdXcHViuCPuvkRrp4xsk3q3HMr13Qp-ID03W3DAsLj3nfluPZ-Wu2xAy1AsiWgOReB9sFghDctLimlrrqyAYpmKmD7xb7dpJcS-rSp9oTUPlSP5bp1Vr7B5buK9BOI0bIykfrp7A/ELnrFqsSBeEk6oznueRlShZ3Y50GJpzN/14>:

For decades ... institutional allocators took roughly the same approach to managing the vast piles of cash under their control: They diversified by divvying up the money across asset classes  for example 40% in stocks, 40% bonds and 20% alternatives  then stuck with it by rebalancing now and again when things got out of whack.

But a growing list of funds is challenging that convention by turning to a method that ditches the asset-class silos. Instead, they pit investments as disparate as, say, public equities and private credit against each other in search of the best bet for the whole portfolio. Dubbed the Total Portfolio Approach, its gaining traction fast  and before month-end it may even be the guiding principle of Americas largest public pension. 

For many such allocators, adopting TPA will mean making drastic changes in culture, governance and infrastructure. Meanwhile there are plenty of skeptics who see little more than a buzzy acronym. But to its proponents, TPA is a better fit than the old static model  known as Strategic Asset Allocation  for an unpredictable world where the likes of inflation spikes or geopolitical shocks can easily upend market assumptions. 

In the platonic ideal of TPA, a board would trust the investment team to make more ad hoc decisions. Staff would freely share information across asset-class teams and would debate whether they should bet on, say, data centers through listed shares or private loans. Quants would dissect the factor exposures of public and private equity alike. The passive benchmarks that previously loomed over every asset class team would be no more. 

If, for example, a PE allocation has risen to 20% from a target of 15%, an SAA investor might be compelled to offload some PE holdings even if liquidity constraints mean pricing is unfavorable. But a TPA fund can cut listed shares instead, since the framework views both as equities driven by similar forces.

It seems obviously true that private equity and public equity are related bets that should in some sense be substitutes for each other, but as a practical matter historically those have been different asset classes managed and overseen by different people, and it was hard to opportunistically move between them. But if they are all just statistical correlations then you might as well try.

South Korean retail investors are contributing to dramatic swings in the share prices of some US-listed companies, as they take aggressive trading strategies long used in their domestic market to a booming Wall Street.

Known for their high-risk tolerance, herd behaviour and use of leverage, South Korean traders have piled into US markets this year, accounting for a significant slice of the trading in some of Wall Streets most volatile stocks. Their holdings of US equities have nearly doubled this year to a record $170bn at the end of October, according to Korea Securities Depository data.

Many have been drawn to the resurgence in meme stocks this year, helping fuel a craze that first took hold during the Covid-19 pandemic. 

Korean retailers are just crazy. They are not like average retail investors in other parts of the world. They are very aggressive, said Jongmin Shim, Korea equity strategist at CLSA. 

Chung Ji-eun  uses a local brokerages mobile trading system and often sacrifices sleep to trade US stocks for about two hours from midnight Korea time because of the 14-hour time difference.

It is so easy to buy and sell US stocks in the system. Dopamine keeps me awake late into the night, she said. You dont even have to convert money yourself. It is automatically done.

It is strange to think that frictionless global markets would cause stock prices to be set by the least rational investors but I suppose that is the working theory here.

FW: 13/11/25: Alle Augen auf die PBB, Sparkassen-Fusion, Apobank
 plant Debt-Fonds
content:
________________________________
From: Finanz-Szene – Der Newsletter <newsletter@finanz-szene.de>
Sent: Thursday, 13 November 2025 06:19:19 (UTC+01:00) Amsterdam, Berlin, Bern, Rome, Stockholm, Vienna
To: Luca Frignani | Exaloan <luca.frignani@exaloan.com>
Subject: 13/11/25: Alle Augen auf die PBB, Sparkassen-Fusion, Apobank plant Debt-Fonds

Außerdem: Wieso operationelle Risiken für Banken neu klassifiziert werden müssen
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/76739326-3b23-34b7-1a12-6c448a7579c1.png]
Anzeige
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/69fd6614-b124-afd1-a646-f535755d8bf5.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=ff5bdf2631&e=8f69674dd2>
Geht's bei der PBB schon wieder um alles? Unser Live-Blog zu den Q3-Zahlen

Was genau ist eigentlich das Problem der Deutschen Pfandbriefbank? Schon klar, als nach der Zinswende der gewerbliche Immobilienmarkt crashte, da gerieten nahezu alle Hypothekenbanken in eine gewisse Verlegenheit. So richtig ins Straucheln kam aber nur eine, nämlich die PBB (siehe im Februar 2024 unser Deep Dive –> Steht die Deutsche Pfandbriefbank wirklich vorm Kollaps?<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=1f0730d05b&e=8f69674dd2>). Und als sich die Risikoergebnisse und damit die Gewinne zuletzt wieder zu stabilisieren begannen (siehe –> Die beste Performance seit langem: Hypothekenbanken lassen Krise hinter sich<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=516350d1af&e=8f69674dd2>) – da war bei einem Player von alldem nichts zu sehen. Nämlich bei der Deutschen Pfandbriefbank. Quasi: Geht's allen Immobanken schlecht, dann geht's der PBB besonders schlecht; und geht's allen Immobanken wieder besser, dann geht's der PBB trotzdem weiter schlecht. Wobei ein bisschen diffus bleibt, warum das so ist. Jedenfalls: Auch dieser Tage hängt über der Deutschen Pfandbriefbank also wieder dieses "Was läuft da eigentlich immer schief?"-Gefühl. Weil Anfang November plötzlich die Aktie crashte. Und sich hinterher herausstellte, dass es vorher sogenannte Pre-Calls mit Analysten gegeben hatte – wobei die bei diesen Gesprächen vermittelten Vibes offenbar nicht die allerbesten waren. Was steckt wirklich dahinter? Gab's im dritten Quartal lediglich einen kleinen Dip, auf den man die Analysten vorbereiten wollte? Oder kracht es schon wieder so richtig im Gebälk? Unser Live-Blog zu den Q-Zahlen kennt die Antwort. Und zwar bis ungefähr 7.50 Uhr. FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=f964dc65bb&e=8f69674dd2>

Anzeige
[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/47c2c8e0-6acb-44b4-ad35-f59b8513040e.png] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=c5a04d1864&e=8f69674dd2>

Für Ehepaare gilt der doppelte Betrag. Wenn Sie sich den Steuervorteil für 2025 noch sichern wollen, muss das Produkt bis zum 12. Dezember 2025 abgeschlossen werden. Jetzt sichern.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=21aa963674&e=8f69674dd2>
Briefing

Exklusiv: Apobank will eigenen Debt-Fonds auflegen – bis zu 750 Mio. Euro Volumen: Als nächstes hiesiges Geldinstitut nach Playern wie der Deutschen Bank, der Helaba oder Berenberg will nun auch die Apobank ins Geschäft mit Debt Funds vorstoßen. Laut Informationen von Finanz-Szene peilt das Düsseldorfer Spezialinstitut für sein erstes derartiges Vehikel ein Fondsvolumen zwischen 500 Mio. und 750 Mio. Euro an – der Zeichnungsschluss ist im ersten Halbjahr 2026 geplant ...

... Um das geplante Volumen stemmen zu können, tut sich die Apobank mit der Deutsche Credit Capital AG zusammen. Dabei handelt es sich um einen in Frankfurt ansässigen Finanzierungs-Spezialisten, der – gegründet 2017 – während Corona in die Insolvenz rutschte und nun im Zuge einer Kapitalerhöhung den Neustart wagt (als CEO firmiert Ex-IKB-Manager Nicolaus Loos, zum AR-Chef wurde kürzlich Credit-Suisse/Flatex-Veteran Martin Korbmacher ernannt, der einzige veröffentlichte Jahresabschluss ist sechs Jahre alt, an der Bafin-Zulassung wird gerade gearbeitet) ...

... Die Korbmacher-Truppe will die Mittel für den Fonds überwiegend bei institutionellen Investoren einwerben, darüber hinaus soll die Apobank ihre Wealth-Management-Klientel angehen. Auch bei der Kreditgenerierung (ein Debt-Fonds braucht schließlich Debt) ist das Heilberufler-Institut zumindest teilweise involviert. Dabei geht es um bonitätsschwächere Kunden, denen die Apobank wegen ihres Risikoprofils (und der damit verbundenen Kapitalbindung) kein eigenes Geld leihen will. Den größten Teil der Forderungen soll allerdings der Partner, also die Deutsche Credit Capital, reinholen.

Ticker

  *   Die Rede ist von einem "Dialog". Aber wenn nicht alles täuscht, dann dürfte daraus die nächste, gar nicht mal so kleine Fusion im roten Sektor werden. News

Founded in 2016, Einride has built a business model that blends its “freight-capacity-as-a-service” offering with a SaaS platform that provides the full ecosystem needed to run electric and autonomous operations.



While the firm has faced some ups and downs — including substantial losses last year and layoffs — it's also enjoyed solid recurring revenue and won regulatory approvals across the US and Europe.



With this move, Einride is positioning itself to scale in the US, where favourable regulatory dynamics and infrastructure could unlock the next chapter of transport innovation. But as the SPAC route remains a challenging path — especially for hardware-heavy, capital-intensive businesses — the stakes are high.

Der Tag

­
[https://cdn.prod.www.manager-magazin.de/images/d1cc8cca-49eb-4994-93f1-454bc8860ae6_w112_r1_fpx51_fpy46.jpg]
Vinzenz Neumaier
Redakteur manager magazin
Lieber Herr Frignani.

Brose-Patriarch Michael Stoschek (77) ist der Typ Unternehmer, den man getrost einen Macher nennen darf. Aus einem kleinen Mittelständler formte er einen Konzern mit mehr als 7 Milliarden Euro Umsatz. Bei Meinungsverschiedenheiten hat Stoschek immer gern das letzte Wort. Zwar wollte sich der Unternehmer eigentlich schon längst aus dem Operativen zurückziehen. Aber, man kennt es, die Sorge um das Lebenswerk ließ einen Ruhestand partout nicht zu. Stattdessen bleibt es auch nach fast 80 Lenzen dabei: Stoschek macht einfach immer weiter.

Zu tun gibt es genug, denn bei Brose läuft es nicht rund. Zuletzt gab es sogar ein dickes Minus. Grund genug für den Brose-Granden, auf Partnersuche zu gehen. Kann vielleicht ein Zulieferer in Familienhand aus Indien in Franken aushelfen?   *   Thomas Coesfeld (35) setzt sich gegen seinen älteren Bruder Carsten Coesfeld (38) durch und wird Chef des milliardenschweren Medienkonzerns Bertelsmann. Die Entscheidung wurde lange vorbereitet  und markiert doch den Höhepunkt einer Karriere im Eiltempo (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12f1311047dd5973c56b1c1fc816ea269b8932f54a5888ea5aeeac85c8db6626d3786caaf4b93851e93b86698591e3a1170525b534bb07ec17>.

  *   Klatsche vor dem Bundesgerichtshof: Wirecard-Aktionäre dürfen ihre Forderungen nicht wie normale Gläubiger im Insolvenzverfahren anmelden. Auch wenn die Eigenkapitalgeber getäuscht wurden, sind ihre Forderungen weiterhin nachrangig<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12c65b2a0610c73d2e434aa9f808a8e0c0e217d35895ddaf410dcac2d484b95b70f5a95f280cd71c8f37d97a90884f053e14aaecbeb7149c2a>. Das Geld ist damit ziemlich sicher futsch.

  *   Des einen Pleite ist des anderen Erfolg. Während Konkurrent Starcar mit der Insolvenz kämpft, hat der Autovermieter Sixt im dritten Quartal weiter zugelegt und mehr verdient. Ausgelassen ist die Stimmung im Landkreis München aber trotzdem nicht  das Unternehmen reduziert seine Umsatzprognose für das Gesamtjahr<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12d6c3f39008e7559364b473e6961e498a3434f911e2f6910a781c038a2b672090db55cdbcd3394ffef2ec639a8615b592b9bdabf81ffdf297>.

[separator]
Was Sie beim Spülen interessieren könnte:

  *   Offenbar bin ich nicht der einzige begeisterte Putzmann, der auf die Marke Frosch schwört. Meine werte Frau Mama hat die Hausflure immer mit den Öko-Mittelchen der Firma Werner & Mertz aus Mainz gereinigt. Ich tue es ihr nach  wenn auch nicht mit derselben Regelmäßigkeit. Reinhard Schneider (57) wird es freuen: Der Geschäftsführer von Werner & Mertz feiert Umsatzrekorde und zeigt der Konkurrenz, dass man auch mit Nachhaltigkeit frisch und erfolgreich sein kann. Der Preis dafür: Schneider wurde zum Entrepreneur des Jahres in der Kategorie Nachhaltigkeit gekürt<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf12cf961ce3b93ea37e659912f4d1d13709d6e8213c0f58e866843a1aad403434cf65eb0ea259ab9c6de9428a047ddd33c0db7ad4bb0c6bdfff>. Zur Feier dieser Nachricht werde ich mit Froschs Anti-Kalkmittel heute Abend erst einmal gründlich meine Badewanne reinigen.

  *   Der Miniwagen Microlino hat zwar den Design Preis Schweiz errungen, dürfte aber optisch kaum jedermanns Sache sein. Die meisten Kundinnen und Kunden schätzen wohl doch eher klassisch-konservative Qualitäten eines Automobils, wie Sitzheizung, Stauraum und ordentlich viel PS unter der Haube. Kein Wunder also, dass der elektrische Zweisitzer bislang nicht zum Verkaufsschlager wurde. Gebaut wird die moderne Version der legendären Isetta von BMW von der Schweizer Unternehmerfamilie Ouboter. Und produziert wird in Italien. Noch. Denn wie Kollege Christoph Seyerlein erfahren hat, droht dem Microlino ohne politische Unterstützung vielleicht bald die Abwanderung nach China (m+)<https://click.angebote.manager-magazin.de/?qs=261a532ec27baf1235adf5aa1d6a0e6ec60931f6d017c1eb4aaf3d4d900f2519a671fdc9d2e10593fb55becac224866fe970a44cc908fb5f411da12372ea73ff>.

Blackstone

If you work in financial markets and are very smart and diligent, you might occasionally notice something weird. Some stock is trading at too high a price, or too low. Some company is being run inefficiently, and if you take it over you can make it worth more. Some company has violated the terms of its bonds<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/D8_L9LuKieiXAoxj_DDRS5Ot72axp37xK7VUgPQfopitqiQDuhPdnXMQ5BxdY5IRXkQwQO5qTFpTS5WBJnUTF8yOq8rIaJmbF1XjNYyYWC2Mwezj2Qcnx9JXIuKsaCIRP_5ivJa5I0PAEv-U9LifyV3-FrxubumjTnBGePjmSmzbYI19NahJ6UQSOxXRuV33mOAUevJUmnQYTxT1_6ZBG4rrxFj-Zs4wzmkMAWZkKYK20XzWlGKd4b9OVUTVdyzO4EbUmjwMLKaY6RYN56TCzFgCe6wOkvjB6ccmk-iVrmwVPnrc2sg_RgnYgSv3dl9pS25NDpsbkzDBHG0xnBzNVm-HunJBKju3x2E8wq9kzT4bNrUKdqBr2sRvJA/-DQ7wWUZtcih-8QlA5b0-4ksSFTyQ8Ms/14>, and if you buy up the bonds<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/mNGqOBTRgEzvb0F9hIB28vPwTVeqqbwbgfdYWp9rAOZilFOy_lQDIoRUw1_w8WpMPC4aXK9Z5tlLijUG6e0c6vj5Y_YS3mkGUuT6vFTCrXF12e0oF69CbzaJOkrVNurYHrnYCDULRqIJ1DqKQwQ_YIkcc8tdmMEIQuh_ZU5uYPPdqGj7DIlvcXSXMtrJiYBUP6j4ka_AFtvOp2gpwsvhJb8WRHtCZmFaeJ55vRaYHNbBXjwevqk0YyDBESQslvMf2iLCra3aXFIt_p1YwzgWem7hRq8QsVVo9zKJHieAR2M6qJDJiuRSOkGo8ct2AV_JNQztZQlpHkLxxbQtMqblBWbpn7tOsPPcRmYeI6azoSG4kHMDfVfVRKwqtA/gBItttlL78zuQyiFsIdZu4zZlkMRp_Fw/14> you can put the company into bankruptcy and extract a lot of value. Some asset is trading at a tiny discount to some economically equivalent asset, and if you buy one and sell the other and lever up the trade you can make some money. The Ruritanian stock market goes up on Tuesdays when it rains, so you should buy Ruritanian stocks on Monday afternoon when the forecast is for rain. All sorts of anomalies and dislocations and inefficiencies and opportunities.

These opportunities have different scales. But this only works with one share; you cannot in any sensible way scale it up. Renaissance Technologies has spent decades taking billions of dollars out of financial markets by noticing anomalies on an industrial scale.

But there are tens of trillions of dollars in the financial markets. Jane Street and Renaissance are big in the sense that they have made billions of dollars for their executives, but in the scale of financial markets the anomalies they exploit are tiny. Somebody can make some money  billions of dollars  by finding weird inefficiencies in financial markets. But everybody cant make all the money that way. In the aggregate, financial markets are not a grand bet on market anomalies; that would make no sense. Everyone cant be noticing inefficiencies that no one else notices; everyone cant be taking money from everyone else by being cleverer than everyone else. In the aggregate, financial markets are a grand bet on global economic growth.

People sometimes divide investing into alpha and beta. Alpha is, approximately, finding opportunities that no one else has noticed and making contrarian bets on them. Beta is, approximately, using your savings to buy a share of global economic growth. BlackRock Inc., the giant asset manager, has more than $13 trillion of assets under management<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/IF01v2zLxFZRyux-cCw4-LPOxcfA_1GAOgE-EKRl_qr9pSQ3tnZpHURO4NGdo3s_hr--ZJp2ECcTjq0yLZQ68PSNijGTP14bSPvjekkH2LWeihsQ7yTeIxeZMpoJ9VsaH601n6DOTEkIOFz_2NVoVZKtNlLHUPmSLTn8eSYG9ZaWsaW0Pk8mz1J9K-3TVzxeocZJFhkMpGAeyiug7NlxJDVT48WK1hAieJlarDSCP69e8ZVqFoZdWtzi-zLcfZscx_NDUE5b9vALTodb3EU-oXevMn10ZzTC_wFap0OGgSs8X1c5rLxycjyTLtu4bZfL1lJXJ2IQ3DiSn9PKfX51ZduegIkIcjMTfm6wr3xVL_v2gpuuLl80RlySv-c/n8GuPEXhu6UD1LnhmQrhCGcIDJ2-7ayg/14>, more than half of which is in index funds and exchange-traded funds. You do not put your money into a BlackRock S&P 500 index ETF because you hope BlackRock will spot clever anomalies. Youre just there for your cut of global economic growth.

Many of the people who got rich and famous in financial markets did so by spotting anomalies. (That tends to work faster than global economic growth.) The most ambitious of them naturally want to scale up: run more money for more people to generate more returns and collect more fees for themselves. This is possible, at some scale. The biggest multimanager multistrategy pod shop hedge funds are essentially industrial anomaly factories: They compete fiercely to hire talented spotters of market inefficiencies, they deploy as much capital as they can against those opportunities, and they scale up by hiring more people to spot more uncorrelated anomalies. Tiny!

Perhaps the greatest financial anomaly-spotting story of the last 50 years is the leveraged buyout. As I have told the story<https://links.message.bloomberg.com/s/c/3tqhoLPtFLYITKrC1u8TtC5q5DTMIfkGj_Ok4c3YorUsLMh8WAJYoodNeW0IXY9-3F_9LznUmEWYV1p1B_HtnmagOl-8DyshBrOcipdd3d0hKNV6lFWB-0DG2SA9zOgxrys6ewmMxBv4H0DcryanV1WQ7qnJOZsL8bjF9ENXN6rtJiXggarQu6e9-Bli1txowDw5V4zOKHPlpLu1DMtUwIvFjlCAJYmo8NU44hvIIRliAgz5FR8rNkv07c9Ed2-AL6F10Kf9AKXuIsdo5BQR5ke3umriL-9IHXm_cYMugzhsJIbRK78-FRxfZpNbF8N8YEzU3P2PygQj_08lsnaCY4ivDfWSwCvT0DRIzgxLPC-BiTfAD9ySiD3CYCg/iv3MCPSXYACC6lOAl81TdK-L_Yz_hi3A/14>, in the 1970s there were a lot of sleepy companies that were lazily run and underlevered, and a small group of pioneers realized that they could borrow money, buy those companies, align incentives, impose financial and operational discipline, flip the companies back to public markets a few years later, make huge profits and keep 20% of those profits for themselves. This opportunity  the market undervalues and underlevers companies, so we can borrow money to buy them ourselves and extract extra profits  turned out to be absolutely enormous. It turned out that you could do leveraged buyouts of companies worth tens of billions of dollars, and this business could support multiple big firms each with hundreds of billions of dollars under management. And those firms could, at least arguably, earn market-beating returns: They gave their investors not just the returns of allocating capital to economic growth, but also the bonus returns of spotting market inefficiencies and correcting them.

So they scaled up. They went from LBO funds to private equity firms to, now, alternative asset managers. They invest in real estate and infrastructure and private credit. Gray also confronted differences of mind when he urged GSO Capital Partners, the credit arm once famed for audacious bets, to come around to his views. Or:

As Gray rallied investment teams around megatrends that were blessed by the top of the house, dealmakers deemed it career suicide to question big sanctioned themes like AI or India, according to some of the employees. Some veterans lamented that the swagger was gone and that investing felt akin to being in a factory or flipping burgers in a line.

Yes: If you run trillions of dollars, you are going to invest in big themes like AI or India. Where can we get access to global economic growth, you will ask yourself, and you will answer with words like AI or India. If your answer is this company has particularly low-priced bonds so if we triggered its CDS with a manufactured default we could make a huge recovery, that is the wrong sort of answer; you are thinking too small. If your answer is we could put some more leverage on this $20 billion public company, even that is now too small. The right sort of answer is AI or India. Your themes have to be big.

So like I want to buy Treasury bonds contingent on the Democrats winning the Senate in 2026 or whatever, a trade where (1) I get the asset if the event occurs, (2) the trade is unwound if the event does not occur but (3) in the interim, the conditional asset itself trades and has a price. One benefit of this is, you know, more ways to manage risk, more ways to speculate, etc. But another benefit is that the prices of the conditional assets could give you information about possible futures: not about how likely the event is, but rather what the effects of the event might be. The price of one barrel of oil contingent on invading Iraq could tell you something about (market expectations about) what invading Iraq would do to oil prices.

After I wrote about shareholder voting yesterday, reader Charles Wang emailed to suggest:

The obvious correct resolution for delegating shareholder votes is to have one publicly traded contract that is a forward contract for the stock conditional on the vote passing and another forward contract for the stock conditional on the vote failing. Then the stock is voted according to whichever side has the better forward price. ...

Really it's a bit bizarre that the markets are supposed to be about efficient allocation of capital but the one thing that's directly about allocation of capital is not settled by the markets.

I suppose that might be manipulable, and for almost all actual shareholder votes the result doesnt matter to the stock price, but I like the general idea.

It would be cool if a business school hired a serial failed entrepreneur to teach a class like How I Started Several Businesses But They Didnt Work. For one thing, there are probably good lessons there: I started a company and did everything right, bask in my glory might be less informative than here are the mistakes I made, figure out how to avoid them. But also one wonders about selection biases. Die Themen diesmal:

#1: Die Pfandbriefbank vermittelt Investoren ein Gefühl, als seien nicht immer alle relevanten Informationen auf dem Tisch

#2: Kosten im Griff, Ziele in Reichweite  die Aareal Bank ist mittlerweile in vielen Punkten das glatte Gegenteil der PBB

#3: Die Deka mag viele Probleme haben  aber es gibt nicht viele Unternehmen, die sich solche Problem so locker leisten können

#4: Bei der BayernLB entschwand von heute auf morgen die Risikochefin. Doch das Risikoergebnis  fällt ganz formidabel aus!

#5: Bei der DKB fragt man sich Quartal für Quartal, wie lange sie ihr Ergebnisniveau noch halten kann. Aktueller Eindruck: noch lang!

#6: Ein Sparkassen-Chef on air  wie wir auf die Geschichte vom überaus lukrativen Goldschatz der Kreissparkasse Biberach gekommen sind

#7: Was die Entwicklung des Core-Bank-Spezialisten Mambu über den Werdegang hiesiger Fintech-Unicorns erzählt

Auf geht's: Finanz-Szene (frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=106af4dbf9&e=8f69674dd2>

[https://mcusercontent.com/44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498/images/1f355e5c-a37c-48c8-869a-69500bd0b72c.jpg] <https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=5ba4764732&e=8f69674dd2>

AI Regulierung  sind Sie bereit? Der EU AI Act zwingt Banken zum Handeln. Wer AI gewinnbringend nutzen will, braucht Regeln, Transparenz und technische Souveränität. Das Whitepaper zeigt, wie es geht  Best Practices inklusive. Jetzt Zugriff sichern.<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=89ec525515&e=8f69674dd2>

Wie die PSD Bank München zur Mutter aller Zinswende-Verlierer wurde (frei zugänglich)

Die Reihen sind eng bestuhlt und dicht besetzt, als die PSD Bank München Ende Juni in einem Innenraum der Augsburger Fußball-Arena ihre Generalversammlung abhält (die PSD Bank München sitzt nicht in München, sondern in Augsburg, darum veranstaltet sie dort auch ihre Mitgliedertreffen). Rund 350 Mitglieder sind angereist, wie im Mittelschiff einer Kirche hat man sie postiert, fünf Stühle rechts, fünf Stühle links, dazwischen nur ein schmaler Gang, kein halber Meter breit, so würde man anhand eines in Umlauf gebrachten Fotos schätzen. Vorne, am Altar, hocken derweil die Großkopferten, es sind mehr als sonst, denn wie die Mitglieder an diesem Abend erfahren werden, nimmt die PSD Bank München ein großflächiges Revirement ihrer Führungsebene vor. Karen Lehmann-Martin, vor fünf Jahren zur Vorstandschefin gekürt, wird sich zeitnah zurückziehen, "aus Altersgründen", wie es heißt, sie ist 61; auch der fürs Kreditgeschäft zuständige Vorstand Jürgen Haschka demissioniert. Stattdessen übernehmen Jens Fischer (bis April noch Chef der PSD Bank Hessen-Thüringen) und Timo Memmer, der von der VR Bank Südliche Weinstraße-Wasgau kommt und zunächst noch als Generalbevollmächtigter firmiert. Ganz schön viele Neuigkeiten also für die Mitglieder, aber das ist noch nicht alles, was sie an diesem Abend erfahren werden. Denn  auch der Jahresbericht liegt zur Lektüre bereit. Und, tja, was soll man sagen: Der hat es in sich! Und zwar in einer Art und Weise, wie es noch selten ein Geschäftsbericht eines deutschen Kreditinstituts in sich gehabt hat. Lesen Sie hier, wie es möglich ist, dass sich die Cost-Income-Ratio einer Bank binnen weniger Jahre von knapp 70% auf 199% (!!!) verschlechtert. Und warum das noch nicht einmal das einzige dramatische Problem der in Augsburg ansässigen Münchner ist  unsere exklusive Recherche aus dem Juli, jetzt für kurze Zeit vor der Paywall: Finanz-Szene (7 Tage frei zugänglich)<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=82e593e04e&e=8f69674dd2>

Blog

  *   Insbesondere Neobroker wie Trade Republic oder Scalable Capital hatten zum Start der Frühstart-Rente auf einen regelrechten Booster-Effekt gehofft. Nun kommt zum Leidwesen der Fintech-Branche alles doch ein bisschen anders. Hier entlang: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=0eb80f5507&e=8f69674dd2>

Ticker

  *   Im Machtkampf bei N26 sind zumindest mal die umstrittenen Aufsichtsratspersonalien entschieden. Aber kehrt damit auch Ruhe ein? Unser Fintech-Ticker: FS Premium<https://finanz-szene.us16.list-manage.com/track/click?u=44c6f60586bc54f2917f00498&id=2a30e5105d&e=8f69674dd2>

Heute im Premium-Newsletter

  *   Die DKB bringt das Kunststück fertig, ihr Zinsergebnis wieder hochzufahren  und verhilft damit der BayernLB zu einem überaus satten Q3-Gewinn
  *   Die Deka steuert aufs nächste Rekordjahr zu  auch, weil sich das institutionelle Geschäft so ein wenig stabilisiert
  *   Ja, es hat für die PBB zu einem kleinen Quartalsgewinn gereicht. Alles in allem bleibt der Garchinger Immobilienfinanzierer allerdings im Krisenmodus
  *   Bei der Aareal Bank bröckelt der Zinsüberschuss so ein bisschen. Aber sonst? Ist man in Wiesbaden in praktisch jederlei Hinsicht auf Kurs
  *   Weiterhin kaum Risikovorsorge  und weiter sinkende Kosten. Die OLB hat auch im dritten Quartal wieder brilliert.

by Tom Nugent

Good morning Luca,



The British Business Bank (BBB) has a treasure trove to deploy between now and 2030. The UK economic development bank, which invests in VC funds and startups, bagged an extra £6.6bn as part of the government’s new industrial strategy, announced over the summer.



A lot of that money will be invested across eight sectors the government defined as “growth-driving” in its summer report, including advanced manufacturing, creative industries, life sciences and clean energy.



A chunk will also go to defence, an area where the bank is looking to do more deals, a trend that has captured European tech in the last couple of years.



Defence and dual-use startups raised €1.85bn last year across 71 deals; so far this year they’ve raised €3.7bn across 126 deals, according to Sifted data.<https://email.sifted.eu/e3t/Ctc/LZ+113/d2mfCN04/VVMNSb4Zh_GwW5RN_xM8nzNZSW3QbRmh5FSM2WN6wcHqY5nR3bW7Y9pgv6lZ3lNW27C2Q321TnByW6ywxzj4ph1_0V6Mjg342VSqQN28xLYR4BTKRVVNHBp8vCZN4W8jnsWn2XW5QMW5hQwrR3D7zn8VNCnCG3blHxfW7nYbmK60C8BDN3kdmPXhdsD7W3mH3yf5NxWLLW9kkChk95FtTBW3cWrSr8pjTVbW233nrj8DdhvtW8hjfBQ18nn3nW6tprBc65PR-SW38zVlV2-RZ8pW742Wdr6ST7y1N9cx8y9VcgzjMby9PHLBqh_Vw3zy57lpXs-W8lS80X298MdSW3GynBS8ffD-nW6zp25w62_---W7mC-TZ8HVN8SW2HQk7Z818l1HW73lxbB2fCyRjW94qLCV2hT56qW92LjzB1X6hNgW11hQQ08g7r82N6KslcJrt1nNN8KbcblLhj7GW1nTzT83vWQ1CW5dNQYq6B5f04W3hjP3n88NC1xW3WQSW48QRG6kW6brJdp7_h4xxW88ZnDH92-L-wW1T93Zg6BnJXzW1MhB1B3Q8nvdW5kWMbr83d79_N67kX0LS3Mn_f979D6W04>



“We’re seeing a lot more defence funds,” Chris Smart, a director in its funds team, tells me at the bank’s office tucked away off Fleet Street in London. “We’re seeing managers that invest more generally looking to do more in defence […] we are seeing more specialists as well, mainly at seed and Series A.”



George Mills, a deeptech-focused director in BBB’s direct and coinvestment team, says he’s also seeing increased dealflow in defence. “There’s more coming in,” he says, “and we’re more open to it than we have been before.”
